function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a CI script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push the repo for you, but the commands below will do it on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo is a simple Node.js app that listens on port **3000** (see `app.js` / `package.json`).  
We’ll use a lightweight Alpine image, install the deps, copy the source, expose the port and start the app.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Metadata
LABEL maintainer="Zelar <dev@zelarhq.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy app source
COPY . .

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *If you prefer the helper function:*  
> ```json
> {
>   "directory_name": ".",
>   "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
>   "maintainer": "Zelar <dev@zelarhq.com>",
>   "expose_port": 3000,
>   "entrypoint": "node app.js"
> }
> ```

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root).

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *If you want the helper function:*  
> ```json
> {
>   "directory_name": ".",
>   "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome-deployment",
>   "image_name": "zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
>   "replicas": 2,
>   "port": 3000,
>   "service_type": "ClusterIP"
> }
> ```

### 2.3 GitHub Actions – CI workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (recommended over password)

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests apply (requires a cluster)
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

That’s it! The repo now contains a production‑ready Docker image, Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image whenever you push to `main`.
